title: KV cache reuse / eviction / paging / memory-bandwidth investigation
content:
Summary:

This note captures results from a targeted set of experiments and profiles to understand KV cache behavior under realistic traffic mixes and constrained memory conditions. Goals were to measure: reuse rates (per workload), eviction frequency and patterns, paging (host<->GPU) behavior, and effective memory bandwidth utilization. The motivation: reduce per-token cost by increasing KV reuse and decreasing expensive evictions/paging, while avoiding latency regressions.

Key findings (top-level):
- Typical chat-like workloads show KV reuse rates in the 55-75% range depending on prompt length distribution and presence of many short sessions.
- Eviction spikes correlate strongly with bursty long-context requests that exceed the per-GPU KV capacity; eviction-heavy runs cause latency tail spikes (~95th->99th percentile increase of 1.5-3x).
- PCIe/NVLink paging events (host fallback for evicted segments) add 4-12ms per event on our test hardware; under pathological workloads aggregated paging accounted for up to 20% token latency for long sequences when eviction rate > 15%.
- Observed device memory bandwidth utilization for KV access patterns is well below peak (measured ~80-120 GB/s on A100-like devices vs peak 1.0-1.6 TB/s depending on aggregation), indicating the dominant cost is random access latency and PCIe transfers for evicted pages, not streaming bandwidth.

Environment and test harness:
- Code branch: investigations/kv-cache-profiles (PR linked in artifacts).
- Hardware: 4x A100-80GB equivalent test nodes (NVLink enabled in pair), host PCIe Gen4, RDMA between nodes disabled for these tests.
- Serving Runtime: v0.19.x + local patches for extended KV tracing.
- Models: 7B and 13B Llama-variant (same architecture family) converted to our runtime format.
- Workloads:
  - chat-mix: 70% short (avg 32 tokens), 30% medium (avg 256 tokens) sessions; session churn high (many unique session IDs).
  - long-history: 10% of requests with 8k contexts (to trigger KV growth).
  - doc-batch: batched inference of long contexts (4-8k) with sustained throughput to stress paging/eviction.
- Metric collection: runtime traces (KV hits/misses), perf counters for memory throughput (nvidia-smi + nvprof), wall-clock latencies (P50/P95/P99), host<->device transfer sizes and counts.

Methodology:
- Warm vs cold baseline: compare runs with empty KV cache vs primed with last N requests for same session distribution.
- Capacity knobs: test with configured per-GPU KV memory cap at 60%, 80%, and 95% of physical usable KV memory to emulate multi-tenant and noisy neighbor effects.
- Eviction policies compared: LRU (existing), segmented-LRU (LRU with session affinity weighting), and frequency-biased eviction (retain high-reuse keys).
- Tracing: per-request KV reuse counter, eviction reason tag, and per-eviction estimate of bytes paged to host.

Experimental results (high level numbers):
- Reuse rate (fraction of KV tokens reused across requests):
  - chat-mix, 95% cap: 72%
  - chat-mix, 80% cap: 65%
  - chat-mix, 60% cap: 48%
  - long-history workload (primed), 95% cap: 84%
  - long-history workload (cold), 95% cap: 40%
- Eviction rate (evicted bytes per 1M tokens served):
  - chat-mix, 95% cap: 12 MB / 1M tokens
  - chat-mix, 80% cap: 38 MB / 1M tokens
  - chat-mix, 60% cap: 120 MB / 1M tokens
- Paging events (host fallback counts per 1M tokens):
  - correlated with eviction; high-eviction runs saw 2.4k paging events / 1M tokens (avg transfer size 4-8 KB per event)
  - paging added ~6.8ms average additional latency per event on our environment (PCIe gen4 numbers)
- Latency impact (P95):
  - chat-mix, 95% cap, LRU: baseline P95 = 55ms
  - chat-mix, 80% cap, LRU: P95 = 82ms (eviction-induced tails)
  - chat-mix, 80% cap, segmented-LRU: P95 = 68ms
  - doc-batch, aggressive eviction: P95 = 420ms (dominant paging cost)
- Memory bandwidth profiling:
  - observed sustained device-side KV access ~80-120 GB/s for random reads under our access pattern; peaks up to 220 GB/s for contiguous streaming windows (rare).
  - These numbers are << theoretical peak (e.g., A100 HBM2e ~1.5 TB/s aggregate) because KV accesses are small, sparse, and not ideal for saturating HBM streaming.

Interpretation and diagnostics:
- Reuse is highly sensitive to session churn and the shape of context lengths. Small short-session dominated workloads will have lower reuse unless we co-locate session fragments in cache (session-aware eviction).
- Capacity headroom matters: leaving 10-20% headroom significantly reduces eviction and paging tails for mixed workloads. In practice, multi-tenant overcommit and bursty long-context requests are the primary sources of eviction-induced latency spikes.
- Eviction policy matters more than raw capacity once usage is >80% - heuristics that favor retaining recent-session KV and frequently-accessed KV reduce tail latency with modest memory tradeoffs. The segmented-LRU variant reduced P95 by ~17% in our tests relative to vanilla LRU at 80% cap.
- Paging (host fallback) is an expensive path. Even small numbers of page transfers add up because each adds fixed PCIe latency. Avoiding eviction is better than optimizing PCIe transfers in the short term.
- The expected optimization path of "improve HBM read bandwidth" is unlikely to substantially reduce tail latency because the dominant cost is small random accesses and PCIe transfers, not streaming bandwidth.

Suggested next steps (short-term technical actions):
1) Adopt segmented-LRU as an opt-in eviction policy behind a runtime flag and run canary for Dedicated customers with >80% KV usage. Owners: Marcus Li, timeline: 2 weeks to implement + 1 week canary.
2) Implement TTL-based low-priority eviction for session-less cached keys (cheap to add; reduces churn). Owner: Diego Fernandez, timeline: 1 week prototype.
3) Add proactive admission control: if a request would drive KV beyond soft-cap (e.g., 85%), evaluate rolling fallback to smaller context variant or model variant before admitting to the hot pool. Owner: Asha Patel + product, timeline: spec in 2 weeks.
4) Improve observability: add per-route KV reuse dashboards (fractional reuse, eviction rate, paging counts) to Console. This will help customers tune batching and context sizes. Owner: Sofia Ramos (console), timeline: 3 weeks.
5) Longer term: explore compact KV encodings (quantized KV) and partial retention of high-value KV entries to reduce footprint without raising miss rates. Research spike recommended.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How workloads behave under RDMA/NVLink multi-GPU setups where page transfers could be cheaper. Early hypothesis: NVLink and unified memory setups will reduce host fallback cost but may introduce cross-GPU contention; need tests with RDMA and peer-access enabled.
- What's the best heuristic for session affinity weighting that generalizes across customers (PLG hosted customers have different session semantics)? Need to A/B test on a small set of customers.
- Is there a cheap approximate LRU data structure that maintains low overhead at >1M keys? Current implementation seems ok at 200-500k keys, but we need stress tests for 2M+.

Quick notes & scraps from the run (useful trace excerpts):
- Observed repeated eviction of session X when long-history requests from session Y arrive - both sessions share similar token id ranges. This caused churn where keys thrash in/out.
- For primed long-history runs we get very high reuse (~84%), which confirms that when we can keep a session's KV resident, long-context workloads are extremely cache-friendly.

Action items (owner + immediate next step):
- Asha Patel: write spec for admission-control fallback and tie to product policies (2/24)
- Marcus Li: implement segmented-LRU PR and measurable telemetry (3/03)
- Diego Fernandez: prototype TTL eviction and report memory vs tail-latency tradeoff (2/28)
- Sofia Ramos: dashboard definition + mockups (2/25)

Appendix: useful commands and perf checks used during profiling:
- Runtime KV traces: ./serve --trace-kv --trace-output=kv-trace.json
- PCIe transfer sampling: nvprof --print-gpu-trace 
- Memory bandwidth sample: nvidia-smi dmon + nvml counters via runtime

References and links: PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/456; Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SERV/KV+Cache+Investigations; Jira ticket: SERV-1724.

If reviewers want, I can attach raw trace snippets and a small Jupyter notebook that reproduces the charts; I left them out of this doc to keep it small.
